title: ETS GRE Analytical Core
subtitle: High-Yield Verbal Reasoning & Critical Contrast
citation: Educational Testing Service (ETS). Official GRE Verbal Reasoning Practice & Standard Academic Vocabulary.
description: Essential lexical discrimination words from the official GRE Verbal Reasoning corpus. Calibrated specifically for high-level textual inference, dialectic reasoning, and logical opposition.

words.definition: Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected.
words.example: Astrophysicists identified an unusual spectral anomaly near the outer perimeter of the nebula.

words.definition: Showing a willingness to take surprisingly bold, unconventional risks.
words.example: The young entrepreneur launched an audacious campaign challenging the dominant tech monopoly.

words.definition: To confirm or give substantial support to a statement, theory, or finding with evidence.
words.example: Forensic auditors found multiple independent receipts that corroborate the witness testimony.

words.definition: Essentially different in kind; not allowing comparison.
words.example: The symposium brought together scholars with disparate viewpoints across anthropology and computer science.

words.definition: Lasting for a remarkably brief or fleeting period of time; transitory.
words.example: Viral internet fame is notoriously ephemeral, often fading within a matter of days.

words.definition: Open to more than one interpretation; intentionally ambiguous or inconclusive.
words.example: The spokesperson offered an equivocal answer that sidestepped the regulatory inquiry.

words.definition: Using very few words in speech or prose; concise to the point of curtness.
words.example: Known for his laconic style, the senior engineer replied to the lengthy email with a single word.

words.definition: To make something bad, dangerous, or painful less severe, hazardous, or intense.
words.example: Redundant server clusters were configured to mitigate the risk of catastrophic database outages.

words.definition: A seemingly absurd or self-contradictory statement that on investigation reveals a deeper truth.
words.example: The paradox of modern productivity software is that it can create more overhead than it eliminates.

words.definition: Dealing with circumstances sensibly and realistically based on practical rather than theoretical rules.
words.example: She championed a pragmatic roadmap prioritizing core usability over experimental features.

words.definition: Not revealing one's thoughts, opinions, or feelings readily; reserved.
words.example: The lead researcher was reticent about premature conclusions before replication completed.

words.definition: To waver or alternate between different opinions or actions; be indecisive.
words.example: Investors continued to vacillate between optimism and caution throughout the volatile trading week.
